The Shore Temple was built from cut blocks of granite stacked together, which is why it is called a structural temple. It came later, around 700 CE, after the rock-cut experiments nearby.

sec.t:
Before the Pallavas, most temples in the south were built of brick, wood and plaster, which rot and crumble. King Mahendravarman I, who ruled in the early 600s, ordered temples to be cut into solid rock instead.

One of his [[inscription|inscriptions]] proudly says that he made a temple without bricks, timber, metal or mortar. He was also a writer. He composed a comic play in Sanskrit, the *Mattavilasa Prahasana*, which pokes fun at drunk monks and squabbling holy men. It is still sometimes performed.

Mahabalipuram's most famous carvings are the Pancha Rathas, five temples carved out of a long [[granite|granite]] outcrop. Each has a different shape: one is like a thatched hut, others like tall towers. Beside them stand a life-size stone elephant, a lion and a bull, carved from the same rock.

Granite is one of the hardest [[@rocks-types|rocks]] to carve. Sculptors used iron chisels and hammers, working from the top down. Some rathas were never finished at the base, which lets visitors see how they worked.

Nearby is a huge carved cliff, about 27 metres long, longer than a cricket pitch. It is known as Arjuna's Penance or the Descent of the Ganga, and experts still debate which story it shows. A natural crack runs down the middle, and it may once have carried water like a river. Around it are more than a hundred figures, including elephants, a cat pretending to meditate and a crowd of mice.

The [[@india-wonder-shore-temple|Shore Temple]] was built around 700 CE under King Narasimhavarman II, also called Rajasimha. Unlike the rathas, it is made of cut granite blocks fitted together. Its slim towers face the Bay of Bengal so that the first sunlight strikes the shrine.

For centuries, sailors used it as a landmark. Salt winds have worn away much of its fine carving, and a sea wall now protects it. After the 2004 [[tsunami|tsunami]], the retreating sea briefly revealed carved rocks and old walls in the sand, and [[archaeologist|archaeologists]] found new carvings along the shore.

Later Pallava kings built the Kailasanatha temple in Kanchipuram, with its rows of small shrines. The [[@cholas|Cholas]], who took over the region in the late 800s, built on these ideas to make even larger temples. The pyramid-shaped towers found across Tamil Nadu today began as experiments in stone on a sandy beach at Mahabalipuram.

text: The reefs around the Andaman Islands are among the richest in India. Hundreds of kinds of hard coral grow here, along with soft corals, sponges and sea fans. Among them live parrotfish, butterflyfish, clownfish in their anemones, moray eels, giant clams, octopuses, reef sharks and sea turtles.

In the seagrass beds nearby grazes the shy dugong, a sea [[mammal|mammal]] that is the official animal of the islands. The Andamans sit far out in the Bay of Bengal, about 1,200 km from Chennai, and much of the sea around them is still clear and less crowded than many mainland coasts. Divers come from all over the world to see them.

st.prompt: What does a dugong mostly eat?

options.t: Seagrass
Small fish
Coral

st.reveal: Dugongs are sea mammals that graze on seagrass meadows near the reefs, a bit like underwater cows. A single adult can eat tens of kilograms of seagrass a day, leaving feeding trails in the sand.

sec.t:
A reef is built by coral [[polyp|polyps]], tiny animals with soft bodies and rings of [[tentacle|tentacles]]. Each one makes a cup of limestone around itself. Millions of polyps side by side, over thousands of years, build a reef big enough to see from a plane.

Most corals live with even tinier [[algae|algae]] inside them. The algae use sunlight to make food and share it with the coral, which is why reefs need clear, shallow, warm water. That is also why they are so colourful. The story of [[@coral-reefs|coral reefs]] everywhere starts with this partnership.

Snorkel off Havelock Island, now called Swaraj Dweep, or in the marine park at Wandoor, and you might see parrotfish crunching coral with beak-like teeth. Their droppings come out as fine white sand. Much of the white sand on reef beaches has passed through a parrotfish.

Giant clams sit open on the reef, their wavy lips glowing blue and green. Lionfish drift with spines spread like feathers. Sea turtles visit to feed, and some islands are nesting beaches for green, hawksbill, olive ridley and huge leatherback turtles, especially in the Nicobar Islands to the south.

There was even a famous swimming elephant. Rajan, a retired logging elephant on Havelock, swam in the sea near the reefs for years and was photographed by divers before he died in 2016.

The dugong grows to about 3 m long and can weigh over 400 kg. It has a whale-like tail and a broad snout for pulling up seagrass. Old sailors' tales of [[@myths-mermaids|mermaids]] may have been inspired by dugongs and their cousins, the manatees.

Dugongs breed slowly, a single calf every few years. Fishing nets, boats and damage to seagrass have made them rare. Only a few hundred are thought to survive in all Indian waters, in the Andamans, the Gulf of Mannar and the Gulf of Kutch.

On 26 December 2004, a giant undersea earthquake set off the Indian Ocean [[@tsunami|tsunami]]. The quake lifted parts of the northern Andamans by a metre or more and dropped parts of the south. Some reefs ended up above water and died. Others were buried in mud. Many have slowly recovered.

A bigger long-term danger is heat. When the sea stays too warm for weeks, corals push out their algae and turn white, called [[@coral-bleaching|coral bleaching]]. The Andaman reefs bleached badly in 1998, 2010 and 2016, and again in 2024. Some recovered, some did not.

Scientists now watch which corals survive heat waves, hoping they hold the key to the reefs' future. The clownfish, at least, has a head start, thanks to a slimy coat that stops its anemone from stinging it, the trick behind every [[@clownfish|clownfish]] home.

text: The Bandra-Worli Sea Link is a 5.6 km, eight-lane road bridge that curves across the Arabian Sea, joining two parts of [[@mumbai|Mumbai]]. It took about nine years to build and opened on 30 June 2009. A trip that used to take 20 to 30 minutes in peak traffic now takes about 10.

Engineers built it in three parts. First they drilled 604 deep holes in the seabed and filled them with steel and [[@cement-concrete|concrete]]. Then they placed hundreds of ready-made concrete pieces on top to form the road. Over the shipping channels, they hung the road from steel cables strung from tall towers. That cable-hung section is what makes it look like a giant harp.

st.prompt: The Sea Link is a cable-stayed bridge. What holds the road up in the middle?

options.t: Steel cables running straight from tall towers down to the road
Big steel arches underneath the road
Floating pontoons on the water

st.reveal: In a cable-stayed bridge, cables run in straight lines from tall towers down to the deck, like the strings of a giant harp. The towers carry the weight down into foundations deep in the seabed rock.

Hindustan Construction Company, Bandra-Worli Sea Link.

Tie threads from the top of the ruler to different points along the card and see how much weight, in coins, it can hold before sagging.

It stands on 604 concrete piles drilled through the seabed into solid rock. The road sits on top of those piles, and over the shipping channels it hangs from cables attached to tall towers.
facts: 604 piles drilled into the seabed rock

sec.t:
Mumbai's sea floor is mud on top and hard [[basalt|basalt]] rock below. That rock came from enormous [[lava|lava]] flows in the [[@deccan|Deccan]] about 66 million years ago. The engineers needed to reach it, because mud can't hold up a bridge.

Workers on barges and temporary platforms drilled holes up to 2 metres wide and pushed them between 6 and 34 metres into the seabed. Each hole was lined, filled with a cage of steel bars and poured full of concrete. These piles act like the roots of a tree. The sea rises and falls about 4 to 5 metres with the [[@tides|tides]] here, and the [[monsoon|monsoon]] brings rough water, so work stopped for weeks at a time.

Where ships and fishing boats pass, the road needed long gaps without piles. Here the engineers built [[@bridges|cable-stayed]] sections. The main tower near Bandra rises about 126 metres. Steel cables fan out from it and hold up a road span of 250 metres on each side, about two and a half football fields with nothing underneath.

The builders said that the steel wire inside all the cables, laid end to end, would stretch about as far as the distance around the Earth. Each cable is a bundle of many thin wires, so the total adds up fast.

Work began in 2000 and was meant to take about five years. It took nine. Court cases, design changes and worries from the Koli fishing families of Worli, whose boats use these waters, all slowed it down. The cost rose from about ₹660 crore to around ₹1,600 crore. Once it opened, cars paid a toll to cross, and tens of thousands of vehicles now use it on an average day.

sec.h: A city that keeps building into the sea
sec.t: Mumbai was once seven islands, and people have been filling in and bridging its sea for 300 years. Since the Sea Link opened, the city has added a new coastal road that joins its southern end. In January 2024, the 21.8 km Atal Setu across Mumbai harbour opened, becoming India's longest sea bridge. Yet the first time India crossed the sea by bridge was more than a century earlier, on a railway line built in 1914 to an island in the south called [[@india-wonder-pamban|Pamban]].

text: London is the capital of the United Kingdom and one of the biggest and oldest cities in Europe. It is famous for its history, from Roman walls to royal palaces. It is also famous for its red buses, black cabs and the Underground, nicknamed [[@metro-trains|the Tube]].

For centuries London was the centre of a huge [[empire|empire]], which is why it is linked with places all over the world, including India. Today about 9 million people live there, and hundreds of languages are spoken in its schools.

st.prompt: In which year did the world's first underground railway open in London?
st.reveal: The Metropolitan Railway opened on 10 January 1863, running about 6 km. Its trains were pulled by steam engines, so the tunnels filled with smoke. Electric trains came later, and today the Underground has more than 270 stations.

myth: Big Ben is the name of the clock tower at the Houses of Parliament.
Big Ben is the nickname of the great bell inside the tower. The tower was called the Clock Tower and, since 2012, the Elizabeth Tower.
facts: by the Romans, around 47 CE, as Londinium

sec.t:
Around 47 CE, the Romans built a bridge over the River Thames and a town beside it called Londinium. In about 60 CE, Queen Boudica of the Iceni tribe led a revolt and burned it. The Romans rebuilt it with a stone wall, parts of which still stand.

In 1066, William the Conqueror took England. He began the White Tower, the heart of the [[@london-tower|Tower of London]], a few years later. The Tower has been a royal palace, a prison and a treasury. The Crown Jewels are kept there. Tradition says that if its ravens ever leave, the kingdom will fall, so at least six are always kept.

In September 1666, a fire started in a baker's shop on Pudding Lane. Most houses were made of wood, packed close together, and a strong wind spread the flames. The fire burned for four days and destroyed about 13,000 houses and the old St Paul's Cathedral.

The architect Christopher Wren rebuilt St Paul's with a great dome, finished in 1710. He also designed dozens of new churches. A tall column called the Monument marks the fire. It is 61 m high, the same as its distance from where the fire began.

By the 1850s, London's streets were jammed with horses and carts. So engineers dug a railway underground. On 10 January 1863, the Metropolitan Railway opened, the first underground railway in the world. Later, deeper [[@tunnels|tunnels]] were dug, round like tubes, which gave the Tube its name.

sec.h: Time, theatre and a famous bell
sec.t:
In 1884, countries agreed that the line of longitude through the Royal Observatory at Greenwich, in London, would be 0°. World [[@time-zones|time zones]] are still measured from it, so Indian time is "GMT plus five and a half hours".

[[@shakespeare|Shakespeare]] wrote and acted in London around 1600. A copy of his open-air theatre, the Globe, was rebuilt near the old site and opened in 1997.

{{story:shakespeare}}

At the Houses of Parliament stands the famous clock tower. The giant bell inside, cast in 1858 and weighing more than 13 tonnes, is nicknamed Big Ben.

The [[@east-india-company|East India Company]] had its headquarters in London, and wealth from India flowed into the city. Many Indians came to study. [[@gandhi|Gandhi]] trained as a lawyer in London from 1888 to 1891, and B. R. Ambedkar studied at the London School of Economics.

In 1810, Sake Dean Mahomed, from Patna, opened the Hindoostane Coffee House, Britain's first Indian restaurant. Today London has thousands of Indian, Pakistani and Bangladeshi restaurants. Indian festivals are part of city life too. Every year, [[@diwali-lights|Diwali]] on Trafalgar Square brings music, dance and food stalls to the centre of London. The city's Neasden Temple, opened in 1995, was built with stone carved in India and shipped over.

text: Nepal is a small country tucked between India and [[@china-today|China]]. Most of it is mountains. In the far north are the high Himalayas, including [[@mountaineering|Mount Everest]]. In the middle are green hills, terraced fields and river valleys. In the south is a strip of flat, warm land called the Terai, which looks much like the plains of Bihar and Uttar Pradesh next door.

Nepal is about 3 crore people strong and very diverse, with over a hundred ethnic groups and many languages. Nepali is the most widely spoken. The country is famous for its mountains, its temples and [[stupa|stupas]], and for being the birthplace of the Buddha.

st.prompt: Nepal's flag is unlike any other national flag. What shape is it?

options.t: Two triangles stacked one on top of the other
A perfect circle
A square

st.reveal: The flag is made of two pennants, one above the other, in crimson with a blue border. The top one holds a moon and the bottom one a sun. Nepal's constitution gives exact instructions for drawing it.

myth: Mount Everest is entirely in Nepal.
The summit sits right on the border between Nepal and China (Tibet). Climbers can approach it from either side, though most go up from the Nepal side.

sec.t:
In about the 5th or 6th century BCE, Siddhartha Gautama, who became the [[@buddha|Buddha]], was born at Lumbini, in what is now southern Nepal. In 249 BCE the emperor [[@ashoka|Ashoka]] visited and set up a stone pillar with an [[inscription|inscription]] marking the spot. It still stands, and Lumbini is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

The Kathmandu Valley is crowded with temples and old palace squares. Pashupatinath, on the banks of the Bagmati, is one of the most important Hindu temples to Shiva. The great white domes of Boudhanath and Swayambhunath stupas are painted with watchful eyes. Hindu and Buddhist traditions mix closely here, and many families honour both.

India and Nepal share a border of about 1,750 km, and it is open. Citizens of the two countries can cross without a passport or visa, and many Nepalis live and work in India, and Indians in Nepal. Gorkha soldiers from Nepal have served in the Indian Army for over a century.

Nepal is also known for never having been ruled by a European power. It was a kingdom for most of its history, until it became a [[republic|republic]] in 2008. Its clocks are set 5 hours 45 minutes ahead of world time, 15 minutes ahead of India. You can find out how countries choose their time in [[@time-zones|time zones]].

The Himalayas are still rising, because India keeps pushing north into Asia. That slow crash builds up stress in the rocks, which is released as [[@earthquakes|earthquakes]].

On 25 April 2015, a magnitude 7.8 earthquake struck central Nepal. Nearly 9,000 people died, and many old temples in Kathmandu's squares collapsed. Since then, many have been carefully rebuilt using the original methods, and new buildings are meant to follow stronger safety rules.

Every other country's flag is a rectangle, or in two cases a square. Nepal's is two stacked crimson pennants with a blue border. The shape is often linked to Himalayan peaks and to the triangular flags long flown at temples.

The moon and sun on it stand for the hope that the nation will last as long as they do. That is the kind of meaning you can explore in [[@flags-world|flag colours]].

text: For hundreds of years, Rajasthan was split into many kingdoms ruled by [[@rajputs|Rajput]] clans, such as the rulers of Mewar, Marwar and Amber. Neighbouring kingdoms often fought each other, and armies from outside the region invaded too. Every ruler needed a stronghold, and a stronghold showed off his power.

The land helped. The Aravalli hills, some of the oldest mountains on Earth, give steep, rocky ridges that are hard to climb. In the west, the Thar Desert made attacks difficult for any army without enough water. Builders placed forts on hilltops, ridges and desert rises, and surrounded them with thick walls. Many still stand, from [[@chittorgarh|Chittorgarh]] to Jaisalmer.

st.prompt: Many Rajasthan forts have huge iron spikes sticking out of their main gates, at about head height. What were they for?

options.t: To stop war elephants from ramming the gates
To hang lamps on during festivals
To tie up horses outside

st.reveal: Armies used elephants to batter down gates. The spikes made that painful, so the elephants refused to push. Some forts, like Mehrangarh in Jodhpur, also built sharp turns before their gates so elephants couldn't build up speed.

src: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Hill Forts of Rajasthan.
Encyclopaedia Britannica, Rajasthan and Rajput.

d.try: Build a model fort from cardboard, clay or sand on a mound of earth or a pile of books. Add a winding entrance path, a wall with lookout points, and a water tank inside. Then ask a friend where they'd try to attack it, and see if your design holds up.
myth: Forts were only military bases where soldiers lived.

Many Rajasthan forts held palaces, temples, markets, homes and huge water tanks. Kings ruled from them, and towns grew up inside and around their walls. Jaisalmer Fort still has homes and shops inside.

sec.h: A wall you can see from far away

sec.t:
An attacking army often didn't try to climb the walls. It surrounded the fort and waited for the people inside to run out of food or water. So builders planned for long sieges.

Forts stored grain in deep stores and collected every drop of rain. [[amber|Amber]] Fort near [[@jaipur|Jaipur]], and many others, used channels, step wells and large tanks to keep water through the dry months. Gates came in a series, one after another, often on a winding uphill path. Iron spikes on the doors stopped elephants from ramming them, and sharp bends meant no enemy could charge straight in. Narrow slits in the walls let [[@archery|archers]], and later gunners, shoot out while staying hidden.

sec.h: The golden fort in the desert
sec.t:
Jaisalmer Fort rises out of the [[@thar-formed|Thar Desert]] like a giant sandcastle. It was founded in 1156 by Rawal Jaisal, and is built from yellow sandstone that glows gold in the evening. It sat on trade routes where camel [[caravan|caravans]] carried goods between India and lands to the west.

What makes it unusual today is that people never left. Thousands still live inside, with homes, shops, temples and small hotels in its narrow lanes. That brings problems: modern water pipes and drains have leaked into the old walls, and parts have crumbled. Conservation groups are working to protect it.

Forts lost their military purpose in the 1800s, when much of Rajasthan came under British influence and cannons got stronger. Many royal families turned parts of their forts into museums or hotels. Mehrangarh in Jodhpur, founded in 1459, now holds collections of palanquins, armour and paintings.

In 2013, UNESCO listed six of the state's hill forts as a World Heritage Site: Chittorgarh, Kumbhalgarh, [[@ranthambore|Ranthambore]], Gagron, Amber and Jaisalmer. They joined India's long list of [[@unesco-sites|World Heritage Sites]], chosen because they show how Rajput builders used hills, rivers and desert for defence. Gagron is unusual: rivers surround it on three sides, so it is a hill fort and a water fort at once. Ranthambore's fort now stands inside a tiger reserve. Visitors climbing to its gates sometimes spot a tiger resting near the old walls, as if it has taken over guard duty.

text: R.K. Narayan was one of the first [[@indian-english-writers|Indian writers in English]] to become famous around the world. He lived from 1906 to 2001 and wrote fifteen novels and hundreds of short stories, most of them set in Malgudi, a small town he made up.

His stories are about ordinary people: a schoolboy who hates arithmetic, a tourist guide who is mistaken for a holy man, a sweet seller worried about his son. Narayan wrote in plain, gentle English with a lot of quiet humour. He rarely judged his characters. He watched them, the way a neighbour might.

Narayan himself

st.reveal: R.K. Laxman, famous for his Common Man cartoons in The Times of India, illustrated Malgudi Days and other books by his elder brother. His sketches also appeared in the title sequence of the 1980s TV series.

Malgudi is imaginary. Narayan built it from bits of Mysuru, Chennai and other places he knew. An old station in Karnataka became a Malgudi museum in honour of the books, but the town in the stories exists only on the page.
facts: born in Madras (Chennai), lived mostly in Mysuru

sec.t:
Narayan was born in Madras, now [[@chennai|Chennai]], and spent much of his childhood with his grandmother there. Later he joined his family in Mysore, now Mysuru, where his father was a headmaster. He was not a keen student and failed his university entrance exam once.

He tried teaching and gave it up after a short time. He decided to become a writer, which in 1930s India was not an obvious way to earn a living, especially in English.

Narayan's first novel, Swami and Friends, follows a ten-year-old boy, Swaminathan, and his gang of friends in Malgudi. Several British publishers turned it down.

A friend studying at Oxford, Kittu Purna, took the [[manuscript|manuscript]] to the English novelist Graham Greene. Greene liked it, recommended it to a publisher, and suggested the shorter pen name "R.K. Narayan". The book came out in 1935. Greene and Narayan stayed friends and wrote letters to each other for the rest of their lives.

Narayan's novel The Guide (1958) is about Raju, a railway-station guide who is mistaken for a holy man. It won the Sahitya Akademi Award, India's top literary prize, in 1960. A Hindi film version, Guide, starring Dev Anand, came out in 1965 and is still loved for its songs.

In 1986, the actor and director Shankar Nag turned Narayan's short stories into a [[@television-invented|television]] series, [[@malgudi|Malgudi Days]], for Doordarshan. Much of it was filmed in Agumbe, a rainy village in the hills of Karnataka. Its hummed theme tune is instantly recognised by millions of Indians who grew up with [[@tv-india|early Indian television]].

Narayan's younger brother, R.K. Laxman, became one of India's best-loved [[@famous-cartoonists|cartoonists]]. For decades his Common Man, a silent figure in a checked coat, watched politics from the front page of The Times of India. Laxman drew the pictures for Malgudi Days.

Narayan wrote in [[@english-spread|English]], and some critics in his lifetime asked whether an Indian writer should. He felt English was simply the language he wrote best in, and he used it to describe Indian life without explaining it for foreigners. He received the Padma Vibhushan in 2000.

The old building of Arasalu, a small railway station in Karnataka that appeared in the TV series, has since been turned into the Malgudi Museum. It celebrates a town that only ever existed in books.

text: Cold [[@breakfast-world|breakfast]] cereal began in the United States in the 1800s as a health food. Doctors and health reformers thought the heavy breakfasts of the time, with lots of meat, eggs and fried food, were bad for [[digestion|digestion]]. They wanted something simple made from grain.

The most famous names were the Kellogg brothers of Battle Creek, Michigan. In the 1890s they invented toasted flakes of wheat and then corn. A rival, C.W. Post, started his own cereal company nearby. Within a few decades, a bowl of cereal with cold milk had become a typical American breakfast, and cereal companies were among the biggest advertisers in the country.

st.prompt: In 1894, how did the Kellogg brothers discover how to make cereal flakes?

options.t: They left some cooked wheat standing, then rolled it out
A machine at a paper factory broke down
They copied a recipe from India

st.reveal: The story goes that cooked wheat was left standing for many hours. When the brothers pushed it through rollers, each grain came out as a thin flake, which they toasted. They later tried the same thing with corn.

d.try: Make a "breakfast survey" in your class or family. Ask ten people what they ate this morning and sort the answers into groups such as cereal, poha or upma, bread, idli or dosa, paratha and other. Draw a bar chart and see which wins.
myth: Breakfast cereal was always a sweet food for children.
The first cereals were plain, bland health foods made for adults at health resorts. Sugar-coated cereals and cartoon mascots came decades later, mostly after the 1940s.

sec.t:
The first ready-made cold cereal was called Granula. It was made in 1863 by James Caleb Jackson, who ran a health resort in Dansville, New York. He baked whole-wheat flour into sheets, broke them up, and baked the pieces again.

The result was rock hard. Diners had to soak the nuggets in milk overnight before they could be chewed. It was not exactly a treat, but it showed people that breakfast could come out of a box.

One of the sanitarium's patients, C.W. Post, started a rival company in Battle Creek. In 1897 he launched Grape-Nuts, which contains neither grapes nor nuts. He said the name came from grape sugar, a name for glucose, and the nutty taste.

Soon dozens of cereal makers rushed into the town. Many failed quickly. The ones that survived spent heavily on [[@advertising|advertising]], toy prizes in boxes and, later, cartoon characters on the front. By the 1950s, sugar-coated cereals aimed at children filled supermarket shelves.

Puffed cereals came from a different idea. In 1901, a scientist named Alexander Anderson found that heating grains in a sealed container and then suddenly releasing the pressure made them burst open. Puffed rice was advertised in the US as cereal "shot from guns".

India had been eating puffed rice for centuries already. Muri in Bengal, kurmura in Maharashtra and pori in Tamil Nadu are made by roasting rice in hot sand until it pops. They go into [[@chaat|bhel puri]] and jhal muri, or are eaten with [[@jaggery|jaggery]]. Poha, rice pressed into flat flakes, is also an ancient ready-to-cook grain.

Kellogg's started selling corn flakes in India in 1994. At first many families poured hot milk over them, the way they would with porridge, and the flakes went soggy fast. Today breakfast cereal shares the table with [[@indian-breakfasts|poha, upma, idli and paratha]].

The word cereal comes from Ceres, the Roman goddess of grain and farming. Whether it is wheat flakes or a plate of poha, nearly every breakfast still begins with her gift. Many packaged cereals contain more sugar than people expect, so [[@food-labels|reading the label]] is worth the effort.
